title: Reporting & Recounting
keyIdea: A spoken report gives facts about one topic; a recount tells something that happened, in time order. For a report, choose facts you can check (not opinions), keep them on the topic and put them in groups, then talk about one group at a time. For a recount, start with who, where and when, tell the events in order with time words (first, next, after that, finally), and end with how it finished or felt. Add descriptive details that show what you saw, heard or felt, and speak clearly at a pace listeners can follow, about 110 to 160 words a minute. If a talk is too long, cut facts rather than speeding up.
familyTip: At tea time, ask your child for a one-minute recount of their day: who, where and when first, then three things in order, then how it ended. Time it on a phone. Next time, ask for one detail that tells you what they saw or heard.

visual.caption: Where does each line go in a recount? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Last Friday, Class 4 went to the zoo.
On Saturday, I went to the park with Gran.
First, we got on the coach.
After that, it started to rain.
Finally, we got home, wet but happy.
In the end, I got my badge and felt proud.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: keep facts on topic, group them, order two recounts, add details that paint a picture and set a clear speaking pace.

kid: A report tells people facts about one topic. A fact is something you can check. Hedgehogs eat worms is a fact. Hedgehogs are cute is an opinion. Leave opinions out, and leave out things that are not about the topic.
Put your facts in groups, like what it looks like, what it eats and where it lives. Then talk about one group at a time. Your listeners can follow you.
A recount tells what happened, in order. Start with who, where and when. Then tell the events. Time words help: first, next, after that, finally. End with how it ended or how you felt.

Add a detail that helps people see or hear it. The waves crashed over our feet is better than it was nice. Speak clearly, not too fast and not too slow. If your talk is too long, cut a fact. Do not just talk faster.
adult: Ages 8 to 11. US Common Core SL.4.4 asks pupils to report on a topic or text, tell a story or recount an experience in an organised way, using relevant facts and descriptive details, and to speak clearly at an understandable pace (SL.5.4 adds sequencing ideas logically). The national curriculum in England sets out the same spoken language aims for all years: give well-structured descriptions, explanations and narratives, and speak audibly and fluently.

A report needs relevant, checkable facts, grouped so the listener can hold them: one sub-topic at a time, often with a signpost (first, they eat...). A recount is chronological: an orientation (who, where, when), events in order joined by time connectives, and a closing that says how it ended or felt. Descriptive details work best when they come from the senses.

Common mistakes: putting opinions (cutest, best) in a report; drifting off topic; listing facts in random order; starting a recount with the most exciting moment so it is out of order; vague details such as nice, fun or good; and racing through a talk that is too long. Careful with pace: about 110 to 160 words a minute is easy to follow (Year 4–5 pupils read aloud at about 130–145 words a minute), and the fix for an overlong talk is to cut facts, not to speak faster.

In the lab your child sorts seven hedgehog cards into use or leave out and groups six facts into three parts of a talk. They order two recounts and choose the most vivid of three details for four sentences. Then they set a speaking pace so three talks are clear and on time, cutting facts when a talk cannot fit.

practice.prompt: Which sentence belongs in a report about frogs?
choices: Frogs lay their eggs in water.
practice.hint: A report gives facts about the topic that you can check.
practice.explain: Frogs lay eggs in water is a fact about frogs. The best pets is an opinion, and football is off topic.

practice.prompt: You speak at {p} words a minute for {m} minutes. How many words do you say?
practice.hint: Each minute you say the same number of words.

practice.prompt: What should the first sentence of a recount tell you?
practice.hint: Listeners need to know what the recount is about before the events.
practice.explain: Start with who, where and when, then the events in order, then the ending.

practice.prompt: Your report has {g} groups of facts with {f} facts in each group. How many facts is that?
practice.hint: Each group has the same number of facts.
practice.explain: {g} groups × {f} facts = {=g*f} facts in the report.

practice.prompt: Which detail paints the clearest picture of a bonfire?
choices: Sparks crackled and floated up into the dark.
practice.hint: Pick the one that tells you what you would see or hear.
practice.explain: Crackled and floated up into the dark tell you what it sounded and looked like. Really good is vague.

pool.prompt: Which time word fits the last event of a recount?
pool.hint: Which word tells the listener you have reached the end?
pool.explain: Finally (or in the end) signals the last event. First starts the events; next is for the middle.

pool.prompt: Sam's talk on volcanoes includes 'Volcanoes are awesome.' What is wrong with it?
choices: It is an opinion, not a fact.
pool.hint: Could you check it, or is it what Sam thinks?
pool.explain: Awesome is Sam's opinion. A report gives facts you can check, like where volcanoes form.

pool.prompt: Your talk is far too long for the time you have. What is the best fix?
pool.hint: Think about what the listeners can follow.
pool.explain: Cut the weakest facts. Talking faster makes listeners miss things, and the ending matters.

pool.prompt: A talk lasts {m} minutes at 120 words a minute. You cut {c} minutes of weaker facts. How many words does the talk have now?
pool.hint: Work out the minutes left, then multiply by the pace.

pool.prompt: Which fact goes in the 'what it eats' group of a talk about foxes?
choices: Foxes eat mice, rabbits and berries.
pool.hint: Which one is about food rather than looks or homes?
pool.explain: Mice, rabbits and berries are food. Bushy tails is about looks; dens is about where foxes live.

pool.prompt: Which is the best order for a recount of a birthday party?
choices: who and when → games → cake → going home
cake → who and when → going home → games
going home → games → cake → who and when
pool.hint: Start with who and when, then follow the time order.
pool.explain: Orientation first, then the events in the order they happened, then the ending.

pool.prompt: A speaker talks at 220 words a minute. What will listeners most likely say?
choices: It was too fast to follow.
pool.hint: A clear pace is about 110 to 160 words a minute.
pool.explain: 220 words a minute is far above a clear pace, so listeners miss facts.

pool.prompt: A report had {t} facts. You cut the {c} that were opinions or off topic. How many facts are left?
pool.hint: Take the cut facts away from all the facts.
pool.explain: {t} − {c} = {=t-c} facts left, all on topic and checkable.
